- Above -2,900 m the block top is about 37 km², and the longest 3.7-km-wide strip on it is about 6 km. Manhattan is 21.6 km long, so it hangs far off the summit.
- Manhattan first fits lengthwise at about the -3,100 m contour (strip 21.5 km).
- It has about 1-2 km to spare at -3,300 to -3,500 m, and about 4.6 km at -4,100 m (strip 26.2 km, area 381 km²).
The narration ('bigger than Manhattan. With room to spare.') is true by area (4-6x). FIX: drape the polygon along the block's long axis over the whole block, down to about the -4,000 m footprint; never place it on the summit area; drop the 20-degree turn and 'room on every side'. Let the spare room show mostly in width.

s111 (6:33) 'Some probably lived here all year round.' The primary sources conflict, and the ledger (C4-07) did not record it. NPS says it is 'likely that individuals ... lived there year-round'; the USFWS Hawaiian Islands refuge page says residents 'likely stayed only a few days or months at a time'. Two agencies give opposite 'likely' claims, and the playbook allows conflicting [!] material only as a hedge that both sources support. FIX: cut s111 ('And people lived here ... Today, nobody does.' still flows), or change it to 'Some may have stayed all year.' and log the conflict in C4-07.

s167 (9:58) 'That's where the Big Island is headed.' It now directly follows 'all the way to Kamchatka ... the sea floor dives back into the Earth', so it reads as a destination. The ledger approved the line (C5-19) for the drowned-atoll fate, not a place. Today's plate motion carries the Big Island west-northwest, toward the Izu-Bonin/Japan trenches. Projected along azimuths 290-305 degrees for about 6,500 km it reaches roughly 27-40N, 140E, not Kamchatka (about 52N, 160E). FIX: make it fate, not place: 'The Big Island is headed the same way.' Or move the line to after s164 ('Past it, every island has drowned.'). Keep the 'KAMCHATKA' label on the peninsula, with at most 'TRENCH' at the chain's end (C5-18).
should_fix: s079 (4:36) 'It covers more of this island than all the other volcanoes combined.' The USGS Mauna Loa page's main text says it 'covers half of the Island of Hawai‘i'; only a video caption on that page says 'just over half' (about 50.5% by area). The claim rests on a 1% margin, and the visual note 'the orange visibly outweighs the rest' cannot be drawn honestly at 50.5/49.5. FIX: 'It covers about half of this island.' and drop 'visibly outweighs'. 'This island' should also clearly mean today's island (the cut to sea level does this).

s084 (4:53) 'See those steps on its side?' In context, 'its' means 'this giant', i.e. Mauna Loa (s075-s083). The documented drowned-reef series (C12-10) is off Kohala, a different volcano, which is where the s083-s084 visual correctly cuts. FIX: 'See those steps on the island's side?'

s104 (6:10) 'Its volcanoes went quiet long ago. Since then, rain has been carving it.' USGS Volcano Watch 2016 (Kauaʻi and Niʻihau tour) says Kauaʻi is a single volcano. Rejuvenated eruptions continued 'more or less continuously for the last 3.5 million years', the most recent about 150,000 years ago, while the canyons formed after the shield stage ended about 4 Ma. FIX: 'Its big eruptions ended long ago. Since then, rain has been carving it.'

s047 (2:46) 'one of dozens of giant slides around these islands'. Moore, Normark & Holcomb 1994 count 68 slides 'from near Midway to Hawaii' along 2,200 km. Around the main islands, USGS 1992 says 'at least 17', and the pullback lights only 8-10 footprints. FIX: 'one of dozens of giant slides along this island chain' (the footprints shown are then clearly a sample).

s062 (3:39) 'Today's shoreline is a thin white line, way up near the top.' From the moat floor, the shoreline sits about 57-59% of the way up Mauna Kea (6,000 m below vs 4,205 m above). At VE 1.0 it will look just past halfway, which contradicts 'near the top' and sits oddly with s002's 'Most of this mountain is underwater'. FIX: 'high up its slopes' or 'more than halfway up'.

s117 visual (6:55): the storm spiral 'sweeps over the lagoon from the southeast'. Per the NHC Tropical Cyclone Report CP012018 (https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/CP012018_Walaka.pdf), Walaka 'moved rapidly toward the north-northeast'; its eye crossed the chain near Brooks Banks, west of the shoals; and its 'eastern eyewall moved across French Frigate Shoals'. FIX: bring the storm in from the south-southwest with the eye passing just west of the atoll (animation must be physically true). The narration 'passed right over these shoals' stays: the eyewall did, and the monument says 'directly passed over'.

s146 (8:41) 'Our fresh-water plant has broken down.' is voiced in the first person as if it were Midway's actual words. Accounts differ on what the message said: 'salt-water evaporators had broken down' (Station HYPO/Symonds), 'water purification system had broken down' (Wikipedia), 'distillation plant' (Parker/NSA), and C5-11 forbids quoting it. FIX: use reported speech, e.g. s145 '...send a message in plain language: its fresh-water plant had broken down.' Keep 'AF is short of water' as the only line voiced as a quote, and caption neither line with quote marks.

s061 (3:36) 'Every ridge down here is real.' This is true only if that shot shows survey-grid relief alone. The HMRG 50 m grid has not been fetched (TLS issue in C12-03), and the look book's U6 adds a foreground normal map. The visual makes it a close pass 'so its detail fills the foreground'. FIX: either guarantee no procedural or noise relief in s061 (real grid only, at whatever resolution is available), or cut the line, which the C12-02 owner-rule flag already suggests.

s204-s205 (12:31) The hand-off ('a whole lake drains down a hole ... Louisiana') is a factual claim with no fact_id. Link it to the Lake Peigneur fact file: in 1980 the lake drained into the salt mine through a drill hole. The line must not imply a cause (MSHA left it undetermined), and the owner must confirm the film is live before it is voiced.

Ch1 number window: 'four hundred' (est. 0:12.9) to 'Two' (est. 1:18.6) is only 65.7 s on the 147-wpm model. If Rodney's real takes run about 9% faster, 3 spoken numbers fall in one 60 s window. Re-check after TTS. The ready fix (C12-14) is 'Not everyone made it out.' in place of 'Two people died.', or drop the spoken year and keep the NOVEMBER 1975 kicker.
s024 (1:21) 'sliding a few yards': the south flank moved up to 26 ft (8 m), about 9 yards (Circular 740 / Volcano Watch 2025). 'Several yards' is the accurate understatement (C12-17b allows it).

s095-s096 (5:37) 'age treats every island here the same way ... And it sinks.' This is a present-tense absolute, while Oʻahu is now rising on the flexural bulge (C12-09a). FIX: 'Over millions of years, age treats every island here the same way.'

Low priority wording:
- s115 'One rock is all that's left of its volcano': in a drain film the volcano's bulk is visibly still there; the USFWS 'last remnant' means above water. Use '...all that still stands above the sea.'
- s170 'Just offshore': HVO says about 19 miles (30 km) south. Use 'Off the south coast'.
- s094 'the baby of the chain': Kamaʻehuakanaloa, introduced at 10:09, is younger. Use 'the baby of the islands'.

result.verdict: REVISE, THEN LOCK. Story and humour score: 7.4/10 against the 8.0 gate. The spine is clear: one drain down one mountain, told as the life of a volcano (collapse, giant, ageing, atoll, grave, birth, true base), and the escalation is real, from 400 ft to Manhattan to Everest to 28 million years to 56,000 ft. Most gags are true, visual and will land with a US audience: "No ferry needed", Manhattan "with room to spare", the Everest climber against the road, "You may have heard that one" with the TRUE stamp, the AF water decoy and COMING SOON. Both human beats mean well. The weaknesses are: (1) the cold open plants no question for the payoff to answer, and the first question-shaped loop comes at 3:13; (2) 0:30-0:52 is overloaded and spends the Midway cut-away reveal early; (3) a paper prop and an abrupt pivot sit around the 1975 deaths; (4) the seal gag's setup comes after its premise; (5) the Hōlei arch tangent lowers the scale at about 84%, just before the payoff; (6) glib wording around the Midway losses, and a paraphrase voiced as Midway's actual message; (7) a soft, repetitive ending whose last line will not stick. The 8 must-fixes are changes of wording and order only; every new line rests on an existing ledger ID. With them the script should clear 8.5. After the edits, re-run draft_tools/build.py for the number windows, the Ch1 cap of 1:30 and the payoff position (87-91%).
must_fix: OPEN LOOP (s009-s010, 0:25-0:31). The cold open answers the title by 0:10 ('Only the top'). Its only forward line is 'step by step', which describes a process and asks nothing. The first question-shaped loop is s055 at 3:13. Add one forward promise right after 'Keep draining. And look down.': 'Even with every drop gone, we won't hit bottom.' (9 words, numberless, no Everest; the claim is C6-04). It creates a paradox the viewer has to resolve. The Ch6 card 'WE HAVEN'T HIT BOTTOM' and s185-s186 pay it almost word for word, which makes the payoff feel inevitable. Fix 2 frees the time it needs.

CH1 DENSITY (s011-s016, 0:30-0:52) and the 0:14 naming. In the retention-critical 30-60 s window the draft stacks 6 ideas (the bank was land, a volcano under coral, the sea rose, the islands sink, the Big Island sinks now, 'slow'). The Penguin Bank cake-cut (s012) also spends Midway's hero reveal (a sunken volcano capped by reef, 7:47) more than 7 minutes early. Cut s012 and tighten to: 'See that flat bank? It was dry land once. / The sea rose after the Ice Age and drowned it. / And these islands sink as they age. / And the Big Island is sinking right now. / Usually, that's slow. Not always.' This keeps both causes (backup-title-2 condition) and saves about 21 words. Also change s004 to 'Now, step by step.' and s007 to 'That's not a what-if. In the last Ice Age, it really happened.', which removes 'one island' said twice in 5 s. That moves the three island names from 0:15-0:18 to about 0:13-0:16, close to the packaging promise map's 'by 0:14'.

1975 RESPECT (s021-s025). (a) The true-scale PAPER basketball hoop stands about 7 s before 'Two people died.' In this film, paper props are the comedy engine (visual_plan S11), so it will read as a gag. Keep the spoken comparison, but draw the hoop as a plain silhouette in the same grade as the scene: no paper edge, no hinge, no SFX. Fade it out before the wave. (b) End the beat on an image, not a cut. After 'Two people died.' (pause 1.4 s to 1.8 s), add 'By sunrise, the palm grove was standing in the sea.' (C12-15: the palms stayed standing in water; it matches the PD Halapē photo already planned). (c) Heard aloud, s024-s025 ('one side of one volcano' / 'a whole side of a volcano') sound like the same phrase twice. Rewrite as 'All that, from a few yards of sliding. / Now picture a whole side of a volcano letting go.' (C12-17b). Never say 'just a few yards', which belittles the deaths. These changes also put the Pali lean gag about 25 s after the deaths instead of 19.

SEAL GAG ORDER (s117-s122). s118 washes East Island away, then s119 introduces the seals resting on the old beach. The picture has to run after, then before, then after again, and the setup arrives after its premise. Reorder: 'This strip of sand was East Island. / Hawaiian monk seals are endangered, and they came here to rest and raise pups. / Then, not long ago, a hurricane passed right over it. / It washed almost all of East Island away.' Then run the GAG in the pause: the seal swims up, finds water, looks left, looks right. Close with 'Since then, the sand has been coming back. / And so have the seals.' Now the picture runs before to after once and the twist lands. Optional stakes line before the hurricane, if the build.py window check passes: 'Only about sixteen hundred are left.' (C4-13).

HŌLEI TANGENT (s180-s184, 10:46-11:04, about 84% of runtime). The scale climbs from 'born at one end, swallowed at the other' down to a 90-ft arch, then back up to the payoff. The ledger also keeps erosion apart from the sinking story, so the beat cannot feed the climax. Move it to Ch4, where it shows the wear-down stage on the Big Island itself, numberless. Change s096 to 'The volcano goes quiet. Rain and waves wear it down. And it sinks.' Then add: 'On the Big Island, the waves have already started. / This September, the sea arch at Hōlei collapsed into the ocean. / Waves had carved it out of lava over centuries.' (C6-10; no cause given, no link to sinking). Ch6 then runs from s179 straight into 'We've drained the whole ocean.' If the owner insists on Ch6 for the host video, cut the beat to that one middle sentence.

MIDWAY LOSSES (s149-s158). 'Badly damaged, it was finished off by a Japanese submarine.' (s153) is video-game language for a ship with a crew. Rewrite it as 'Already crippled, it was sunk by a Japanese submarine.' Put a 1.2 s pause and the music cue change after s149, because the comedy beat 'AF = MIDWAY' with a thunk currently runs straight into the battle. Cut s157 ('A research ship has filmed each of them.'). It is a provenance aside wedged between 'more than three miles down, on the deep ocean floor' and 'These are war graves, for American and Japanese sailors alike', and the war-graves line needs to follow the wrecks directly.

AF DECOY (s146-s148). Truth: 'Our fresh-water plant has broken down.' is voiced in first person, as if it were Midway's actual message, but accounts word it differently (C5-11: evaporator, distillation plant or desalination). It is a paraphrase delivered as a quote. Humour: casual viewers need one word to see the trick land. Rewrite: 'The bait: Midway's fresh-water plant had broken down. / Japan bit. A coded Japanese report passed it along. / AF is short of water. / That confirmed it. AF was Midway.' Only 'AF is short of water', the standard translation, stays quote-like.

ENDING (s198-s205). After the payoff, the draft narrates the refill shot by shot ('The trench fills first. Then the slopes. Wave by wave, the postcard comes back.'). It also says 'giant' 3 times and 'postcard' twice in about 12 s, and the last sentence stumbles on 'into ... into'. The hand-off answers a 'what happens' question with a place ('It happened in Louisiana'). Rewrite: 'Now put the ocean back.' [about 12 s of refill under music, no words] / 'And the giant disappears again.' / 'Every postcard of the Big Island shows only the top of a giant.' / 'One that's slowly sinking into its own dent in the planet.' / 'So next time you see one, look down.' / 'And what happens when a real lake drains, straight down a hole? Louisiana found out.' The last story words are now the title's own '(Look Down)'. The line keeps C6-09b's Big Island scope and repeats no statistic. 'A real lake' also frames our drain as the thought experiment it is.
should_fix: PALI OPENING (s027-s033). Cut s028: it is a camera look-down 8 s before the real dive at s030 and steals that dive. Cut s033 ('Hawaii's volcanoes don't just grow...'), which restates the Ch1 ending 30 s later. Keep 'Pali means cliff' (one second of respect for the language). Use one hedge instead of two: s031 becomes 'If you've stood here, you've stood at the edge of something huge.' and s032 keeps its 'may'. Taste: frame the lean gag so the stone wall or railing stays between the tourist and the drop; he leans into the wind, never out over the edge (1795 battle, C12-18).

NUʻUANU (s044-s048). Two 'not just one' escalators sit 7 s apart ('And that's just one block.' / 'And this isn't the only one.'), and 'debris' is said 3 times. Cut s044 and s046, so the beat runs: 'With room to spare. / The debris runs for more than a hundred miles. / And it's one of dozens of giant slides around these islands. / They lie on the sea floor, out of sight. / They're rare. But they happen.'

KĪLAUEA TIE-BACK (s051-s054). 'Toward the sea' is said twice in 5 s, and s054 ('Instruments on the flank record that motion nonstop') is flat and reads as a data-provenance line under the owner's ban. Cut s054 and make s052 'And it's still on the move.' so that 'Not falling. Creeping.' becomes the button (add a small music dip so it plays as the dry laugh in the 2:35-4:12 gap).

MID-FILM SAG (s081-s097, 4:44-5:45). 'Here's the twist.' and 'Here's how it works.' are signposts 33 s apart, and 'already moving' does not feel like a twist. Rewrite s081 as 'But this giant can't stay.' and drop 'Here's how it works.' from s090. The hot-spot glow cut-away appears at s081-s082 and again at s090-s093: show it once and let the candle carry the explanation. There is also no laugh for about 100 s, from the road gag (4:19) to the hat callback (6:03), right in the usual mid-film dip. A cheap, true fix: s094 'That makes the Big Island the baby of the chain. A very big baby.' with a crash zoom out on the word.

TIME MACHINE (s098-s116). Turn s100's awkward 'Maui's joined island' into a paid loop: 'Remember that joined island from the start? At its biggest, it was larger than today's Big Island.' s103-s104 say 'carved' twice; merge them into 'Older still: Kauaʻi. Its volcanoes went quiet long ago, and rain has carved it into canyons.' Cut s116 (the La Pérouse naming aside): it is a fourth name beat in about 9 s and a weak gag. Optional: cut s099 (Haleakalā) to save a proper noun.

NIHOA (s110-s113). In 'Archaeologists have found dozens of sites here, even graves.', the word 'even' makes the graves sound like a bonus find. 'Some probably lived here all year round.' then hedges the beat's best moment. Rewrite: 'Centuries ago, they built homes, farm terraces and shrines on this rock. / And they buried their dead here.' (pause 1.0 s, no SFX) / 'Today, nobody lives here. It's a protected refuge.' (C4-07 lists the burial sites.)

DARWIN AND METAPHOR CONSISTENCY. s137 'And he never came here.' and s160 'Darwin never saw it.' say the same thing about 85 s apart; cut s137 and keep the Kure version, which pays off with the blue map. s168 'every story on this conveyor' brings in a third metaphor after the candle-and-paper and the plate; use 'But every volcano in this chain had to start somewhere.' Cut s127 ('a long way northwest of Honolulu'), which is filler.

PAYOFF POLISH (s176, s187-s193). Give COMING SOON's tag its own beat: 'Opening date: thousands of years from now. [0.3 s] At least.' s193 and s194 say 'true base' twice in 4 s; change s193 to 'Look down. Past the old sea floor. All the way to the bottom of the dent.' and keep 'from its true base' in s194 (mandatory qualifier). Pay the trench loop in words as well as in the picture: after 'It sits in a dent.', add 'That trench at its feet is the edge of it.' (have the fact-checker confirm the 'edge' wording against C3-04 before lock).

LENGTH TRADE. Together, the cuts above remove about 35-40 s before the payoff. Do not let the film fall below 12:45, and keep the 56,000 line at 87-91%. Win the time back with story, not padding: the must-fix additions (the loop line, the grove line, the Hōlei move to Ch4, 'Japan bit'); the monk-seal stakes line (C4-13); longer pauses on the two death beats and on 'never get to see' (2.0-2.5 s); and, if still short, reserve line C12-11 (the Hilo drill) in place of s086 as a sharper proof of sinking, after the build.py window check.

OWNER CALLS. (1) 'Every ridge down here is real.' (s061). From the story side, keep it: it lands on awe and names no data, source or method. Never add the sonar clause; the owner has the final word. (2) An optional fourth appearance of the recurring paper tourist: in the final frame he peers over the postcard's bottom edge on 'look down'. It is a light, memorable button, nowhere near a death or a grave, and inside the niche report's 2-4 appearances.
